name: Ganguro

card.summary: A Japanese gyaru style built on a deep tan, bleached hair and white eye and lip makeup, used to create a high-contrast, bold face.
card.note: Traditional versions relied on repeated UV tanning, which the WHO's cancer agency classifies as a known carcinogen.

quick.overview:
Ganguro is a fashion and makeup look from Japan's gyaru youth culture. It pairs a very deep tan with bleached or silver hair, white concealer used as eyeshadow and lipstick, black eyeliner and false lashes. Wearers use it to make the eyes and lips stand out sharply against dark skin.

The style began in the mid-1990s in Tokyo, centred on Shibuya, and peaked in the late 1990s. It was deliberately set against the pale-skin ideal in Japanese beauty. A paler trend called bihaku replaced it around 2000, and offshoots such as yamanba carried the high-contrast look further.
quick.how: The look is assembled from layers: tanning (salon, sprays or dark foundation), bleached or dyed hair from orange to silver-grey, pale concealer on the lips and around the eyes, heavy liner, lashes, face gems and bright clothing. Gyaru magazines such as egg and Popteen served as style guides.
quick.risks: The main documented risk is repeated artificial tanning: the WHO's IARC classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen, and meta-analyses link indoor tanning to higher melanoma risk. Frequent bleaching can also damage hair. Tan can be approximated with makeup instead of UV.

lead: Ganguro is a style from Japanese gyaru youth culture in which young women pair a deep tan with bleached hair and high-contrast makeup. The look uses dark skin as a backdrop for white-lined eyes and lips, long lashes and bright accessories, giving a deliberately bold face [1].

The style grew from the gyaru subculture in the mid-1990s, centred on Tokyo's Shibuya and Ikebukuro districts. Wikipedia describes its originators as rebellious youth who rejected the traditional ideal of pale skin. It peaked in the late 1990s and had largely faded by about 2000 as the light-skinned bihaku trend took over [1]. Grokipedia gives a similar account and dates the peak of mainstream visibility to around 1999 to 2001 [2].

Practitioners achieved the tan through tanning salons, sprays and dark foundation. Research on indoor tanning describes elevated risks of skin cancer and skin ageing, which is the main health context for the original version of the style [3].

chain: Deep tan (UV, spray or dark foundation)
Bleached hair and white eye and lip makeup stand out against it
angle.text: Ganguro changes the look of the face by darkening the skin and then outlining the eyes and lips in pale tones. Wearers use the contrast to make their features appear larger and more graphic. The tan can be built with makeup rather than UV.

paras: The name is usually explained as coming from ganganguro or gangankuro, loosely translated as a burn-black or dark-tanned look. Typical elements are a deep tan, hair dyed red to blonde or silver-grey, black ink eyeliner, white concealer used as lipstick and eyeshadow, false eyelashes, plastic facial gems and pearl powder. Clothing tends to be bright, with platform shoes, miniskirts, tie-dyed sarongs, face stickers and heavy jewellery [1].
A Japanese pop culture subculture, it sits within gyaru, where each substyle has its own name. Ganguro is sometimes called kuro gyaru (black gyaru).

Wikipedia dates the trend's start to the mid-1990s and places its centre in Shibuya and Ikebukuro. Its early adopters are described as defying the traditional Japanese concept of beauty, which favoured pale skin [1].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes ganguro as developing from the kogyaru school-uniform look and gives the heart of the scene as the Shibuya 109 department store area, with the magazines egg and Popteen amplifying it [2]. The figures it cites should be read with care, since the two sources date the peak slightly differently.

Magazines made individual stars. Buriteri, named after black soy sauce, was among the earliest and best-known ganguro figures; egg magazine promoted her, and she later retired from the scene after negative press [1]. Ageha and Popteen also covered the style [1].

By around 2000 the singer Ayumi Hamasaki's light-skinned image helped drive the bihaku craze, which displaced ganguro [1]. An extreme offshoot, yamanba (named after a mountain witch of folklore), grew out of it; by 2008 the 'manba' version featured darker tans, bright synthetic hair and dreadlock-style extensions [1].

Individuals have kept the look into later years. Wikipedia mentions a woman profiled in 2017 who had worn it for over a decade and described herself as one of few remaining followers [1]. Grokipedia says elements were absorbed into other gyaru formats aimed at working women [2].

The look historically depended on repeated UV exposure. The WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen. A 2014 meta-analysis summarised on Wikipedia's tanning bed page found indoor tanners had a 16 percent higher melanoma risk, and higher still for those who began young. Burns, skin ageing and eye damage are also documented, and many countries restrict tanning-bed use by minors [3].
Makeup-only versions of the tan avoid UV exposure. Repeated bleaching of hair is also associated with dryness and breakage.
No studies found on ganguro itself. Related research on indoor tanning is summarised above [3].

timeline.event: Ganguro emerges in Shibuya and Ikebukuro as a gyaru substyle [1].
Peak popularity, promoted by magazines such as egg [1][2].
Pale-skinned bihaku trend, associated with Ayumi Hamasaki, largely replaces it [1].
Manba / yamanba offshoots show darker tans and synthetic hair extensions [1].
